what_its_for: Alglucosidase alfa is used to treat Pompe disease (also called glycogen storage disease type II). Pompe disease is a rare condition where your body cannot break down a sugar called glycogen, causing it to build up in your muscles. This buildup makes your muscles weak, including the muscles you use to breathe. This medicine replaces the missing or poorly working enzyme (called GAA) that your body needs to break down glycogen.
how_to_take: This medicine is given as an intravenous (IV) infusion, meaning it goes directly into your vein through a needle or catheter. It is always given by a nurse or healthcare provider in a clinic or hospital setting — you cannot give this to yourself at home. Each infusion takes several hours, so plan ahead and bring something to keep yourself comfortable (a book, headphones, snacks). You will be watched closely during and after the infusion for any reactions.
dosing: The usual dose is 20 mg per kilogram (kg) of your body weight, given once every 2 weeks. Your doctor will calculate the exact dose based on your weight. The infusion is given slowly at first, and the rate may be increased gradually if you tolerate it well. Your healthcare team will let you know exactly how long each infusion will take.
missed_dose: If you miss or have to reschedule your infusion appointment, contact your doctor or care team as soon as possible to set up a new appointment. Try not to go too long between doses, as staying on schedule helps the medicine work its best. Do not try to double up on doses to make up for a missed one.
storage: This medicine is stored and handled by your healthcare provider or specialty pharmacy. You do not need to store it at home. For your information: the medicine must be kept in the refrigerator between 36°F and 46°F (2°C and 8°C). Once mixed (reconstituted), it must be used within 24 hours. It should never be frozen or shaken.
what_to_avoid: Tell your doctor about ALL medicines, vitamins, and supplements you take, as some may affect how this drug works. Avoid starting any new medicines without checking with your doctor first. Do not skip infusion appointments, as missing doses can allow glycogen to build up again and worsen your symptoms. If you have ever had a serious allergic reaction during a previous infusion, do not ignore it — always tell your care team before your next dose.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or go to the emergency room right away if you experience: trouble breathing or shortness of breath, chest pain or tightness, rapid or irregular heartbeat, severe dizziness or fainting, swelling of the face, lips, tongue, or throat, hives, rash, or severe itching, high fever or chills, or feeling very flushed or hot during or after the infusion. Also call your doctor if you notice your muscle weakness getting worse, have trouble swallowing, or develop any new or unusual symptoms between infusions.
when_it_works: Alglucosidase alfa does not cure Pompe disease, but it can slow down how fast the disease gets worse. Some patients notice improvements in muscle strength and breathing over time, while for others the goal is to slow further decline. It may take several months of regular treatment before you notice changes. Your doctor will do regular tests (like breathing tests and walking tests) to check how well the medicine is working for you.
special_populations: Children and Infants: This medicine is approved for patients of all ages, including newborns and infants. Babies with the most severe form of Pompe disease often show the fastest benefits when treatment is started early. Pregnant or Breastfeeding Women: Tell your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. The effects of this medicine during pregnancy are not fully known. Talk to your doctor to weigh the benefits and risks. Older Adults: Older patients can use this medicine, but should be monitored closely during infusions. Patients with Heart Problems: Pompe disease can affect your heart, and your doctor will monitor your heart health throughout treatment.
